cards.name: Bhojpuri / Awadhi flavour for Bihar and UP audiences
cards.summary: A light seasoning of Bhojpuri or Awadhi words, address forms and rhythm on top of ordinary bolchaal Hindi, written in Devanagari, for readers in eastern UP, Bihar and Jharkhand. Good flavour reads as warm and local; a full dialect script written by a non-speaker reads as mockery.
use_for: festival and local-pride campaigns for Bihar and eastern UP (Chhath, Holi, Sattu season, wedding season) where a few local words signal 'this is for you'
regional reels, voice-over hooks and WhatsApp forwards for Purvanchal audiences
greeting lines, CTAs and sign-offs ('रउआ सब', 'सब बढ़िया बा') inside otherwise standard Hindi copy
music, film and folk-culture content where Bhojpuri is the native register (with a native reviewer)
avoid: Writing whole paragraphs in dialect unless a native speaker writes or signs off the piece: use standard Hindi plus two or three markers instead.

Using the dialect to mock its speakers (the stock 'rustic bhaiya' joke): satire that targets the speaker, not the situation, is a reputational risk; write the character as smart and let the dialect be incidental.
Blending Bhojpuri, Awadhi, Maithili and Magahi forms as if they were one 'Bihari' language: choose one variety per piece and one reviewer who speaks it.
Dialect in legal, price, eligibility or safety lines: keep those in clear standard Hindi so nothing is misread.

sources.title: Bhojpuri language (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: spoken in eastern UP, western Bihar, northwestern Jharkhand and diaspora; about 50.5 million speakers in Census 2011 with more counted under Hindi; Devanagari is the main script (historically Kaithi); large cinema and music industry

sources.title: Awadhi language (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: spoken in the Awadh region of UP; grouped under Hindi by the government; Ramcharitmanas is in Awadhi

rules: Script is Devanagari. Kaithi is the historical script and is not used for modern copy; do not write Bhojpuri in Roman letters unless the audience's own captions are Roman (then follow lang:hinglish_roman house spelling). (src: Bhojpuri language, Wikipedia)

Flavour, not dialect: keep the sentence frame, verbs and numbers in standard bolchaal Hindi (lang:hindustani_everyday) and drop in a few dialect markers. Rule of thumb for a checkable limit: no more than one marker per sentence and no sentence that is entirely dialect. (house practice, unsourced)

Typical Bhojpuri markers a writer can use only after a native speaker confirms them for the piece: रउआ / रउरा (respectful 'you'), हमनी (we), बा (is), कइसन (how), केतना (how much), काहे (why), 'का हाल बा?' as a greeting. Awadhi has its own forms (for example 'का हो'); do not mix the two sets in one piece. (examples from general usage, not from the sources above; verify with a native speaker)

Pick one variety per piece: Bhojpuri (western Bihar, eastern UP, Jharkhand) or Awadhi (Awadh region of UP). The two are different languages that the government groups under Hindi. (src: Awadhi language, Wikipedia)

Spell every dialect word one way across a series and keep a small house list (same idea as a Hinglish spelling list, see lang:hindi_romanisation_schemes); dialect spellings are not standardised, so inconsistent spellings look like errors.
Keep brand names, product names, prices and legal text in standard form; dialect goes in greetings, reactions, sign-offs and one hook line.
Every dialect piece gets a native-speaker read before it ships; record the reviewer's name in the job notes. A single wrong marker is read by locals as an outsider trying too hard.
For voice-over, give the TTS or the voice artist the Devanagari spelling of the dialect word and a Hindi gloss in brackets in the working script; remove the gloss from the final text.
mistakes: Whole-script dialect by a non-speaker (a 150-word Bhojpuri ad written from a dictionary). Fix: standard Hindi with two or three confirmed markers.
'Bihari' treated as one language, so Maithili or Magahi words land in a Bhojpuri line. Fix: name the variety in the brief and have a speaker of that variety review.
The dialect speaker is the butt of the joke (the slow villager, the gullible bhaiya). Fix: make the speaker the one who spots the trick; keep the humour on the situation.
Dialect inside a refund, eligibility or health line, so a reader unsure of a word misreads the condition. Fix: put terms and conditions in plain standard Hindi.
Same word spelled three ways in one campaign (बा / बाऽ / baa). Fix: one house list, checked in the style sheet (edit:style_sheet).

Roman-script 'Bhojpuri' written phonetically for Instagram with no Devanagari anywhere, so search and voice-over both suffer. Fix: Devanagari as the master text, Roman only for a caption if the page already writes Roman.
cards.sample: छठ आ रहा है, तो ठेकुआ में असली गुड़ ही पड़ना चाहिए। रउआ पटना की हमारी दुकान पर आइए, बिना मिलावट वाला गुड़ चख के देखिए। सब बढ़िया बा, एक बार लेके तो देखिए। दाम सीधा है: एक किलो पर 20 रुपये कम, छठ तक।

cards.name: Simplified English for subtitles and captions
cards.summary: English timed text is condensed speech, not a transcript: at most two lines of 42 characters, shown at a speed a viewer can read (up to 20 characters per second for adults, 17 for children), with line breaks that follow grammar and numbers set by one rule. These are Netflix's published numbers; use them as the professional default.
use_for: English subtitles for Hindi or Hinglish reels, films, interviews and explainers
English closed captions for YouTube and OTT deliveries
burn-in captions on reels where the limits of the platform allow the same two-line, 42-character pattern
checking a vendor's SRT or VTT before it goes to a client
avoid: Using Netflix's numbers as the limit for a social platform's own caption field: that is the platform's card (for example plat:instagram_caption), not this one.
Verbatim transcription of speech: condense instead (the Netflix guide favours reduction and condensing to keep reading speed under the limit).
Adding italics for plain emphasis; reserve them for the cases the guide names (narration, inner monologue, lyrics, unfamiliar foreign words, titles).

sources.title: Netflix English (USA) Timed Text Style Guide
sources.supports: 42 characters per line, max two lines; up to 20 characters per second for adults, 17 for children; numbers 0-10 written out, above 10 as digits (ages always numerals); break after punctuation and before conjunctions and prepositions; do not split article-noun, adjective-noun, first-last name, subject-verb, preposition-verb, verb-auxiliary; dual speakers marked with a hyphen and no space; smart ellipsis U+2026 for pauses of 2+ seconds; italics only for narration, inner monologue, lyrics, unfamiliar foreign words, electronic dialogue, titles; times as 9:30 a.m.

rules: Maximum 42 characters per line and two lines per subtitle; keep to one line when the text fits. (src: Netflix English USA)

Reading speed ceiling: 20 characters per second for adult programmes, 17 for children's. Arithmetic you can check: a subtitle on screen for 3 seconds may hold 60 characters, 2 seconds 40. If it is longer, cut words, do not shrink the font. (src: Netflix English USA)

Condense: drop fillers ('you know', 'basically', 'like'), repeated words and tag questions; keep the meaning, names and numbers. (src: Netflix guide's preference for reduction; the filler list is house practice)

Break lines after punctuation and before conjunctions and prepositions. Never split an article from its noun, an adjective from its noun, a first name from a last name, a subject from its verb, a preposition from its verb or an auxiliary from its verb. (src: Netflix English USA)
Numbers: zero to ten spelled out, 11 and above as numerals; ages always numerals; exact times as '9:30 a.m.'. Example: 'nine orders', '12 orders', 'he is 7'. (src: Netflix English USA)
Two speakers in one subtitle: a hyphen with no space before each line ('-Are you coming?' / '-In a minute.'). (src: Netflix English USA)

Pauses of 2 seconds or more and trailing speech use one ellipsis character (U+2026), never three full stops; do not use an ellipsis to join a sentence split across two subtitles. (src: Netflix English USA)

Italics only for narration, inner monologue, song lyrics, unfamiliar foreign words, electronic dialogue (speaker off screen) and titles; never for names, places or companies, and never for plain emphasis. (src: Netflix English USA)
Pick one spelling variety for the whole file (lang:us_english, lang:uk_english or lang:indian_english) and one spelling per Indian name; keep a name list for the project (edit:style_sheet).
Sound cues, when included, go in square brackets in lower case, and only when the sound is not visible on screen. (src: Netflix English USA)
mistakes: Subtitle copies the Hindi line word for word and runs at 28 characters per second. Fix: condense to the core claim and keep the timing; check characters per second per cue, not on average.
Three-line cue, or a 60-character single line. Fix: split into two cues at a clause boundary.
Line break leaves 'the' at the end of line one. Fix: move the article down with its noun, or reflow so the break falls after a comma or before 'and'/'to'.
Mixed numbers: 'five orders' in one cue, '5 orders' in the next, '12' beside 'twelve'. Fix: apply the 0-10 / 11+ rule everywhere, with ages and times as the exceptions.
Italics used to stress a word ('this is *really* important'). Fix: leave plain; stress belongs in the performance.
Hinglish words transliterated three ways across a series ('yaar', 'yar', 'yaaar'). Fix: one spelling in the project name list; italicise only if the word is likely unfamiliar to the audience.
Three dots typed with the full-stop key. Fix: one ellipsis character U+2026.

cards.name: Global / plain English for non-native readers
cards.summary: Short, literal, idiom-free English written for readers whose first language is not English and for text that machine translation or a translator will process next. Good global English has one word per idea, one idea per sentence, and nothing a dictionary-and-translation tool would mangle.
use_for: source copy that will be translated into Hindi or other Indian languages (the base text for transcreation)
help-centre, onboarding and policy text for an international or multilingual audience
B2B pages and decks sold to buyers across Asia, the Gulf and Africa
emails and product copy where readers use English as a second or third language
avoid: Flattening brand voice: for hooks, taglines and jokes, do not simplify; mark them for transcreation (lang:transcreation) instead of forcing them through plain English.
Dumbing down expert content: plain does not mean childish; keep correct technical terms and define them once.
Using it for an audience that reads English natively and expects voice: pick the local variety (lang:indian_english, lang:us_english) and the right tone card.

sources.title: Microsoft Style Guide: Global communications
sources.supports: assume readers whose first language is not English and content that will be machine-translated; defines translation vs localization; points to plainlanguage.gov and the Global English Style Guide (Kohl, 2008)

sources.title: Google developer documentation style guide: voice and tone
sources.supports: global audience: simple consistent language, minimal culture-specific references, no figurative language

sources.title: Best Practices for Localisation of e-Governance Applications in Indian Languages, v5.7
sources.supports: avoid slang, colloquialisms and obscure phrasing in source text: hard to translate, can offend

rules: Write for a reader whose first language is not English and assume the text will be machine-translated. (src: Microsoft global communications)

No figurative language and no culture-specific references: cut metaphors, idioms and sport or festival comparisons ('hit it out of the park', 'touch base', 'Diwali-sale energy'). Say the literal thing. (src: Google style guide, tone)
No slang, colloquialisms or obscure phrasing in source text; they are hard to translate and can offend. (src: e-Governance localisation best practices)

One term per concept for the whole piece (not 'plan', 'package' and 'subscription' for the same thing); put it in the glossary before writing. (src: consistent terminology principle; see tech:consistent_terminology)
One idea per sentence; aim for sentences under about 20 words and break anything longer. (house practice, unsourced)
Prefer a plain verb to a phrasal verb: 'cancel' not 'call off', 'postpone' not 'put off', 'continue' not 'carry on'. (house practice, unsourced)
Name the subject: repeat the noun instead of leaning on 'it', 'this' or 'they' across sentences; machine translation guesses wrong when the antecedent is unclear. (house practice, unsourced)
Dates with the month as a word ('5 October 2026') and amounts with a currency name or code ('INR 12 lakh (1.2 million rupees)'); state units for any lakh/crore figure. See lang:india_locale_formats.

Mark every line that must be adapted rather than translated (taglines, puns, rhymes, CTAs) and hand it to transcreation; plain English is the safe base, not the creative line. (src: Microsoft translation vs localisation distinction)
mistakes: Idioms and sport metaphors in source copy ('step up to the crease', 'low-hanging fruit'). Fix: literal wording ('start now', 'the easiest first step').
Indianisms in a global piece: 'prepone', 'do the needful', 'revert back', 'out of station'. Fix: 'move earlier', 'please take this action', 'reply', 'away'. See lang:indian_english.
Long noun stacks: 'customer data privacy policy update notice'. Fix: 'a notice that we updated how we keep your data private'.
Same product called three names across a page. Fix: glossary first, then search-and-check.
A joke or pun in a support article that the translator must explain. Fix: cut it or flag it for transcreation.
Writing 'Rs 5 lakh' for a reader who does not know a lakh. Fix: add the plain number or a conversion on first use.
cards.sample: To change your delivery address, open Orders and select the order. Select Edit address. Type the new address and select Save. You can change the address until we pack the order. After we pack it, the courier delivers to the old address. If the order is already packed, contact support and give your order number.

cards.name: English for Gulf NRI audiences
cards.summary: Indian-English copy written for the roughly 8.9 million NRIs counted by India's Ministry of External Affairs across the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar and Bahrain. The audience is sourced; there is no published style guide for this variety, so the writing rules below are working practice, marked as such.
use_for: remittance, banking, insurance and property-back-home campaigns aimed at Indians working in the Gulf
festival and community offers (Onam, Eid, Diwali, Pongal, Ugadi) for Gulf Indian shoppers, restaurants and grocery chains
travel, flight and visa-service ads for Gulf residents flying to India
education and job-portal copy where the reader is a Gulf resident or a family member in India
avoid: Treating the six countries as one market: rules, currencies, holidays and platform habits differ; write per country when the offer is regulated or priced.
Putting audience-size claims in a deck without the source: use the MEA figures and name them.
Making financial, legal or visa claims without a compliance check: a remittance rate, an insurance benefit or a visa promise must be verified and dated before it is written.

sources.title: Ministry of External Affairs (India): Population of Overseas Indians (table, undated in the text layer)
sources.supports: NRIs: UAE 3,419,875; Saudi Arabia 2,592,166; Kuwait 1,028,274; Oman 779,351; Qatar 745,775; Bahrain 323,292

sources.title: Indian numbering system (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: Indian publications use lakh/crore for rupee amounts and international units for foreign currencies

rules: Cite the audience with the MEA table, not a search summary: UAE 3,419,875; Saudi Arabia 2,592,166; Kuwait 1,028,274; Oman 779,351; Qatar 745,775; Bahrain 323,292 NRIs, which add up to 8,888,733 (about 8.9 million) across the six countries. The table's date is not shown in the text layer, so write 'MEA figures' and not a year. (src: MEA Population of Overseas Indians)
Base variety is Indian English with British spelling (lang:indian_english); change to the client's own house style if it writes -ize or American forms. (house practice, unsourced)

Show rupee amounts for the family in India in lakh/crore (see lang:india_locale_formats) and Gulf-currency amounts in international units with the ISO code (AED, SAR, KWD, OMR, QAR, BHD); never write a Gulf price with lakh-style grouping. (src: Indian numbering system, Wikipedia, for the lakh/rupee versus international-unit split; currency codes are house practice)
Quote any exchange rate with the date and the provider it came from, or leave the rate out. (house practice, unsourced)

Write the Gregorian date for every deadline and offer end; if a festival moves with the lunar calendar (Eid, Ramadan), say the expected Gregorian date and 'subject to moon sighting'. (house practice, unsourced)

Keep the copy culturally neutral for a mixed Gulf audience: no alcohol, pork, dating or political references in promotional lines unless the client and country team confirm the placement allows them. (house practice, unsourced; confirm per country)

Do not assume English is the reader's first language: the Gulf Indian workforce spans many home languages, so for a big spend commission a transcreated version per language (lang:regional_indian_languages, lang:transcreation). (house practice, unsourced)
Regulated claims (remittance fees, insurance, investments, visa services) need a compliance read in the country of the reader before publish; flag them in the job notes. (house practice, unsourced)
mistakes: Quoting a different audience size from a search summary. Fix: use the MEA table and name it.
Pricing a Gulf offer as 'AED 1,50,000'. Fix: international grouping for foreign currency ('AED 150,000').
'Pay in 2 days' with no timezone or banking-day note. Fix: say the working days and the cut-off in the sender's country.
A festival offer that ends on a lunar date written as a weekday only. Fix: the Gregorian date plus the weekday.
One English ad for a Malayali, Tamil and Hindi-speaking audience in the same city. Fix: brief a native transcreation for each segment.
Using Indian-only references (state cricket teams, Indian taxes) for a reader who lives and pays in the Gulf. Fix: use references the reader meets daily.
cards.sample: Missing the Onam sadya this year? Order a full sadya from our Sharjah kitchen and we deliver it hot to your door. Book by Friday and pay AED 65 per meal. Offices and labour camps can order in bulk, and pickup points stay open from 11 am. Your family in Kerala can send a gift sadya to a relative the same day.

cards.name: Hindi in Devanagari (standard)
cards.summary: Standard written Hindi: the polite aap-form in formal and UI copy, purna viram (।) for the full stop, Latin digits 0-9, dates as '25 सितम्बर 2016', brand names left as they are, and spelling that follows the Central Hindi Directorate standard (postpositions joined to pronouns but not to nouns, anusvara for a nasal before its own class, chandrabindu where Hindi needs it).
use_for: websites, apps, product UI, emails and government-style notices in Hindi
news, explainers, brochures and press notes where a standard register is expected
base text that a voice-over, subtitle or SEO writer will adapt (lang:hindi_voiceover_tts, lang:hindi_subtitles, lang:hindi_seo)
proofreading any Hindi deliverable against one spelling standard
avoid: Using the formal aap/यह/वह rule on reels and creator content: there 'तुम'/'तू' is often a deliberate tone choice (see tone:desi_casual_hinglish); the rule is for UI and formal copy.
Typing the danda as a pipe, the letter l or a Latin full stop: it is U+0964.
Heavy Sanskritised words in copy for a general audience: use the everyday register (lang:hindustani_everyday).

sources.title: Mozilla style guide: Hindi (hi-IN)
sources.supports: use आप/यह/वह not तुम/ये/वे; avoid curt imperatives (ढूँढें not ढूँढो); purna viram (।) not '.' or '|'; Latin digits 0-9 not ०-९; brand names neither translated nor transliterated; dates like 25 सितम्बर 2016; time as 10:30 बजे

sources.title: Devanagari Lipi evam Hindi Vartani ka Manakikaran, Central Hindi Directorate, 2024 edition
sources.supports: spelling standard: postpositions joined to pronouns and separate from nouns; anusvara for nasal before its own class (पंकज, गंगा, संध्या) but not when doubled (अन्न, सम्मेलन); chandrabindu in Hindi words and feminine plurals (लड़कियाँ, महिलाएँ); verb forms गए/गई; hyphen in dvandva compounds; visarga adverbs (अतः, पुनः); Constitution Art. 343(1) international form of Indian numerals for Union official purposes. Rules were read from the PDF text layer, which is garbled on this machine: verify against the printed edition

sources.title: Danda (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: danda U+0964 and double danda U+0965; Hindi uses them together with Western punctuation

sources.title: Hindustani language (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: standard Hindi is the Sanskritised register of Hindustani; grammar and core vocabulary are shared with Urdu

sources.title: Netflix Hindi Timed Text Style Guide
sources.supports: Modern Standard Hindi, no dialect words; no space before punctuation marks; bindu may replace chandrabindu in subtitles

rules: Politeness: use आप, यह, वह rather than तुम, ये, वे in formal and UI copy; use polite imperatives (ढूँढें, not ढूँढो). (src: Mozilla hi-IN)

Full stop is the purna viram '।' (U+0964), never '.' or a pipe '|'. Question mark, exclamation mark, comma, hyphen, colon and quotes are the Western marks; only the full stop changes. (src: Mozilla hi-IN; CHD 2024; Danda, Wikipedia)
Do not leave a space before punctuation: 'है।', 'क्या?', not 'है ।'. (src: Netflix Hindi timed text)
Digits are Latin 0-9, not ०-९. (src: Mozilla hi-IN; CHD 2024 cites Constitution Art. 343(1), the international form of Indian numerals for Union official purposes)
Dates are day month year with the month in Devanagari: '25 सितम्बर 2016'. Time takes a colon: '10:30 बजे'. (src: Mozilla hi-IN)

Brand, product and company names are not translated or transliterated: write 'Firefox', 'Swiggy', 'Tata' in Latin even inside a Devanagari line (exception: a voice-over script, see lang:hindi_voiceover_tts). (src: Mozilla hi-IN)

Postpositions (ने, को, से, का, में, पर) are written separately after a noun: 'राम ने', 'सेवा में'. After a pronoun they are joined: 'उसने', 'आपने', 'तुमसे', 'मुझको'. With two postpositions the first joins and the second stands apart: 'उसके लिए', 'इसमें से'. If ही or तक comes between, the postposition is separate: 'आप ही के लिए'. (src: CHD 2024)
Anusvara (ं) stands for a nasal before a consonant of its own class: पंकज, गंगा, चंचल, संध्या, मंदिर, संबंध. Keep the written nasal when it is doubled: अन्न, सम्मेलन, सम्मति. (src: CHD 2024)

Chandrabindu (ँ) is required where it changes meaning (हँस / हंस, अँगना / अंगना) and in feminine plurals ending in a, ā, i, ī, u, ū: लड़कियाँ, महिलाएँ, वस्तुएँ, रीतियाँ. Where a vowel sign sits above the headline (में, नहीं, क्यों), the bindu is written as an anusvara. (src: CHD 2024)

Verb forms गए / गई, किए, लिए, आए (not गये, किये, लिये) for the past-tense verb; adjectives keep their own spelling (नया, नयी, नये). (src: CHD 2024; Mozilla's own example text still shows 'किये गये', so this is a choice to settle per client in the style sheet)

Compound verbs stay as separate words: 'जा सकता है', 'पढ़ा करता है'. 'वाला' is separate after a verb or demonstrative ('करने वाला', 'यह वाला') and joined as a noun suffix ('घरवाला', 'टोपीवाला'). 'कर' joins the verb: 'पाकर', 'खा-पीकर'. (src: CHD 2024)
Hyphen in paired (dvandva) words: 'राम-लक्ष्मण', 'खाना-पीना', 'लेन-देन'; none in most tatpurusha compounds: 'रामराज्य', 'राजकुमार', 'गंगाजल'. (src: CHD 2024)
Tatsam adverbs keep the visarga ः: अतः, पुनः, प्रायः, वस्तुतः, क्रमशः. (src: CHD 2024)
Write 'श्री' and 'जी' separately when they are an honorific ('श्री गंगाधर', 'महात्मा जी') and joined when part of a name ('श्रीराम'). (src: CHD 2024)
English sounds: use ऑ (ardhachandra) for the open o of doctor and college: डॉक्टर, कॉलेज, ऑफ़िस (see lang:hinglish_devanagari). (src: CHD 2024)
Reflexive possessive with आप: write 'आप अपने ... ' not 'आप आपके ...' when the subject owns the thing (Microsoft Hindi style guide; Central Hindi Directorate 2024 standard). (lead fix 2026-10-07)
mistakes: Full stop typed as '.' or '|' in a Hindi paragraph. Fix: replace with '।' (U+0964); search the final file for ' | ' and '.' at line ends.
Devanagari digits in UI or prices, or a mix of ६ and 6 on one page. Fix: Latin digits throughout.
'उस ने', 'आप ने' (pronoun with a separate postposition) next to 'रामने' (noun with a joined one). Fix: join after pronouns only.
Using तुम or the imperative '-ो' form in a bank or government notice. Fix: आप and '-ें' forms.
A brand name transliterated in running text ('स्विगी') in UI or print copy. Fix: keep the Latin brand name; transliterate only in a voice-over script.
Nasal confusion: 'हंस' for the verb 'हँस' (laugh), or 'महिलायें'. Fix: follow the chandrabindu rule; 'महिलाएँ'.
Hindi lines pasted from another tool with the danda as the letter 'I'. Fix: check the code point; one global replace to U+0964.
Mixed spellings of the same word across a document (गये / गए). Fix: pick one in the style sheet and run a find-and-check.
cards.sample: आपका ऑर्डर 25 सितम्बर 2026 को भेजा गया था, और अब यह आपके शहर पहुँच चुका है। कृपया कल 10:30 बजे तक अपना पता जाँच लें। अगर कुछ ग़लत है, तो हमें लिखें, हम तुरंत सुधार करेंगे। धन्यवाद।

cards.name: Romanising Hindi: Hunterian, IAST/ISO 15919 and informal Hinglish spelling
cards.summary: Pick the romanisation for the job. Hunterian (India's national scheme for geographic names) for places and official names; IAST or ISO 15919 when the Devanagari must be recoverable; ITRANS or Harvard-Kyoto for ASCII-only pipelines; and plain informal Hinglish spelling, with no diacritics and one house spelling per word, for social copy.
use_for: deciding how to spell Hindi names, places and titles in English copy, captions and subtitles
building the house spelling list for a Hinglish series (kya, hai, nahi) so every post matches
romanising shlokas and Sanskrit terms for an educational or scholarly piece (lang:sanskrit_iast)
naming files, slugs and tags in plain ASCII
avoid: Diacritics (ā, ṭ, ś) in social captions: most readers do not type them and the text becomes unsearchable; use informal spelling instead.
Hunterian for anything that must be turned back into Devanagari: it does not mark retroflex versus dental letters.
Overriding a person's own spelling of their name with a scheme: use the spelling on their handle, passport or byline.

sources.title: Devanagari transliteration (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: Hunterian is India's national romanisation for geographic names but does not mark retroflex vs dental; IAST is losslessly reversible; ITRANS and Harvard-Kyoto are ASCII schemes; informal romanised Hindi dominates online

sources.title: International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: IAST diacritics (macrons for long vowels, underdots for retroflexes, ś ṣ ṃ ḥ), its relation to ISO 15919 (IAST ṛ vs ISO r̥; ISO marks ē ō), capitalisation of proper names allowed

rules: Choose the scheme by job. Names of places and official bodies: Hunterian. Scholarly, devotional-reference or reversible text: IAST (or ISO 15919 when one scheme must cover several Indian scripts). ASCII-only systems (filenames, code, plain-text search): ITRANS or Harvard-Kyoto. Social and reel copy: informal Hinglish spelling. (src: Devanagari transliteration, Wikipedia)

Hunterian loses the retroflex/dental distinction (ट vs त, ड vs द, ण vs न), so it cannot be reversed to Devanagari: keep the Devanagari original next to it when the exact word matters. (src: Devanagari transliteration, Wikipedia)

IAST is lossless: long vowels take a macron (ā ī ū), retroflex consonants an underdot (ṭ ḍ ṇ ṣ), plus ś, ṃ, ḥ, ṅ, ñ and vocalic ṛ. ISO 15919 follows IAST closely; it writes vocalic r as r̥ and marks long e and o as ē and ō. (src: IAST, Wikipedia)

IAST diacritics allow capital letters on proper names; ASCII schemes (ITRANS, Harvard-Kyoto) use capitals as code, so never let their capitals leak into public copy ('kaa' or 'RRi' for का, ऋ). (src: IAST, Wikipedia; Devanagari transliteration, Wikipedia)

Social copy never uses diacritics. Keep one informal spelling per word across a series, and write the list down: hai/hain, nahi (not nahin/nai), kya, kyun, bahut. (src: Devanagari transliteration, Wikipedia, for the informal norm; the list is a house choice)
Write Hindi words as spoken: a Hindi word drops its final inherent 'a' (kamal, not kamala), while Sanskrit in IAST keeps it (kamala). (general usage, unsourced)
Personal names follow the person's own spelling; place names follow the current official spelling. (house practice, unsourced)
Never feed Roman Hindi to a Hindi voice or TTS engine: give it Devanagari (lang:hindi_voiceover_tts). (house practice; see lang:hinglish_devanagari)
mistakes: Sanskrit mantra posted with Hunterian-style spelling ('pashyantu') in a scholarly caption, losing ś. Fix: IAST for the reference line, Devanagari for display.
'Nahi', 'nahin' and 'nai' all used in one caption series. Fix: one spelling in the house list.
Diacritics pasted into a reel caption where the font lacks them, showing boxes. Fix: informal spelling for the screen, IAST only in the show notes.
ITRANS-style 'aa' and capital letters ('raam', 'Rama' mixed) in public copy. Fix: informal spelling that readers recognise.
A surname respelled by the writer ('Sharma' to 'Sarma') for 'consistency'. Fix: keep the person's own spelling.
Using the Roman spelling as a TTS script. Fix: Devanagari script for the voice, Roman for the caption only.
cards.sample: Aaj ka plan simple hai: subah chai, dopahar mein kaam, shaam ko sunset. Kal bhi yahi karenge. Kaun kaun saath hai? Comment mein batao, hum sabko tag karenge. (House list: hai, nahi, kya, mein, saath; no diacritics.)

cards.name: Hindi and Hinglish SEO
cards.summary: Write Hindi pages for how Indians really search: Devanagari pages ranked on the visible text, Hinglish queries typed in Roman letters, one language per page and one URL per language. Indic-language use is mass-market (870 million users, 98% of Indian internet users, accessed the internet in Indic languages in 2024), and Google fills thin Hindi results with translated English pages, so original Hindi content has room to rank.
use_for: Hindi versions of service, product and local pages for Indian small businesses and D2C brands
Hindi blogs, explainers and FAQs aimed at 'sarkari yojana', money, health and exam queries
keyword briefs that must list both Devanagari and Roman queries (lang:hinglish_roman) for the same topic
YouTube and Shorts titles and descriptions in Hindi or Hinglish
avoid: A translated English page with no Hindi keyword research: write for Hindi intent (tech:search_intent_matching) and transcreate rather than translate.
Side-by-side English and Hindi on one URL: give each language its own URL.
Claiming a share of Hindi versus Hinglish searches: no primary source for script-wise search share was found; say 'research both' instead.

sources.title: Google Search Central: Managing multi-regional and multilingual sites
sources.supports: Google determines page language from visible content, not the lang attribute or URL; separate URLs per language; avoid side-by-side translations

sources.title: IAMAI and Kantar, Internet in India 2024
sources.supports: 870 million users (98% of internet users) accessed the internet in Indic languages in 2024; 57% of urban users prefer Indic-language content; online search is among the activities done in Indic languages (chart)

sources.title: Search Engine Journal: Google Updates Indian Searches With Translated Results (2021)
sources.supports: Google translates English result titles and snippets into Hindi and other Indian languages because local-language content is scarce

sources.title: Hinglish (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: a cited YouTube-comment study found Romanised Hindi far more common than Devanagari; Google supports Hinglish in Gboard and Search

rules: Research every target keyword in both scripts ('sarkari yojana' and 'सरकारी योजना'), using Search Console queries and autocomplete, and record both in the brief. (src: batch note; Hinglish, Wikipedia)

One language per page. Write the Hindi page on its own URL; do not put English and Hindi translations side by side, because Google judges the page language from the visible text, not from the lang attribute or the URL. (src: Search Central multi-regional sites)
Link the Hindi and English counterparts to each other with the hreflang annotations Search Central describes for localised versions. (src: Search Central multi-regional sites)
Write the title, H1 and first paragraph in the script that the main query is typed in; put the other script once, naturally, in an FAQ question or a bracketed alias, not as a keyword string.

Write original Hindi, not a machine-translated copy: Google already translates English results into Hindi because local-language content is scarce, so a faithful translation adds nothing for the searcher. (src: Search Engine Journal)
Use the standard spelling of the main keyword (lang:hindi_devanagari) in headings; add a common alternative spelling only in body copy if Search Console shows people use it.
Titles and descriptions: Devanagari renders wider than Latin, so judge truncation in a search-result preview, not by character count alone (plat:google_search_result). (house practice, unsourced)
Keep URL slugs in short Latin letters ('/sarkari-yojana-list'); Devanagari in a URL turns into percent-encoded text when copied. (house practice, unsourced)
Use Latin digits and, for rupee amounts, the formats in lang:india_locale_formats, so a number in a snippet matches how people search for it.
mistakes: Hindi page built by translating the English one, with the English keyword translated word for word ('सरकारी योजना सूची' when people type 'yojana list'). Fix: take Hindi and Hinglish queries from Search Console and autocomplete first.
English and Hindi paragraphs stacked on one URL. Fix: two URLs and hreflang.
Only Devanagari keywords researched for a topic where most queries are typed in Roman letters. Fix: check both scripts and place the Roman variant in a heading, FAQ or alias.
Meta description in Hindi cut mid-word in the result. Fix: preview it and shorten.
Claiming 'Hinglish gets X% of searches' in a pitch deck. Fix: cite only what a source shows (the IAMAI-Kantar Indic-language figures) or say the split is unknown.
cards.sample:
Title: GST नोटिस का जवाब कैसे दें: जयपुर के CA की 5 स्टेप गाइड
H1: GST नोटिस मिला है? पहले ये 5 काम करें
Meta: GST notice का जवाब देने की आख़िरी तारीख़, ज़रूरी दस्तावेज़ और आम ग़लतियाँ। जयपुर के CA ने सरल हिंदी में समझाया।
पहला पैराग्राफ: GST नोटिस आने पर घबराइए मत। पहले नोटिस की तारीख़ और धारा देखिए, फिर जवाब की आख़िरी तारीख़ कैलेंडर में लिख लीजिए।

cards.name: Hindi subtitles and on-screen text
cards.summary: Hindi timed text follows Netflix's published rules: 42 characters per line, two lines at most, up to 22 characters per second for adult programmes (18 for children's), numbers 1-10 written as words, English words transliterated into Devanagari, no italics, and on-screen text subtitled only when the story needs it.
use_for: Hindi subtitles and captions for films, series, interviews and YouTube videos
burn-in Devanagari captions on reels and Shorts
translating English dialogue into Hindi timed text
reviewing a vendor's Hindi SRT before delivery
avoid: Breaking a line inside a word or conjunct: break at word spaces only.
Treating Netflix numbers as the limit for a social platform's own caption field: that is the platform's card.
Dialect words in subtitles: Netflix asks for Modern Standard Hindi.

sources.title: Netflix Hindi Timed Text Style Guide
sources.supports: 42 characters per line, max two lines; up to 22 characters per second for adults, 18 for children (SDH 25 and 20); bottom-heavy pyramid, avoid one or two words on the top line; numbers 1-10 written out, above 10 as digits, sentence-initial numbers spelled out; ordinals 1-9 as words and 10वीं, 12वीं as digits plus वीं; times with a colon; currency transliterated without symbols (10 डॉलर); English words transliterated; no space before punctuation; smart ellipsis U+2026; no italics, quotes for titles; dialogue hyphen without a space; on-screen text only if plot-pertinent; Modern Standard Hindi, bindu may replace chandrabindu

rules: Maximum 42 characters per line and two lines per cue. (src: Netflix Hindi)
Reading speed up to 22 characters per second for adult programmes and 18 for children's; closed captions for the deaf and hard of hearing allow 25 and 20. (src: Netflix Hindi)

Count characters as code points including matras and spaces, to stay safe: a Devanagari line that looks short can be long in characters. The guide does not say how it counts, so keep a margin below 42. (house practice; the guide's counting method is not stated)

Prefer a bottom-heavy line shape (shorter top line); do not leave one or two words alone on the top line. Break only at word spaces so no conjunct or word is split across lines. (src: Netflix Hindi; word-boundary rule is house practice)

Numbers: 1 to 10 as words (एक, दो, तीन); 11 and above as digits; a number that starts a sentence is written as a word; ordinals 1-9 as words (पहला, दूसरा, नौवाँ) and 10 upward as digits plus वीं (10वीं, 12वीं); decades keep the numeral (20 का दशक). (src: Netflix Hindi)

Decimals use a full point (16.8); large numbers use commas (50,000); clock times use a colon (8:30). For amounts of a lakh and above write words ('5 लाख') rather than guessing the grouping. (src: Netflix Hindi; the lakh note is house practice, see lang:india_locale_formats)
Currency: transliterate the unit without a symbol: '10 डॉलर', '20 पाउंड'; by the same pattern write '10 रुपये', not '₹10'. (src: Netflix Hindi; rupee case follows the same pattern)
English words used inside a Hindi line are transliterated into Devanagari with correct spelling: 'वेरी सॉरी'. No special marker needed. (src: Netflix Hindi)

No space before punctuation; the closing quotation mark follows the full stop; the ellipsis is the single character U+2026 and is used for pauses of 2 seconds or more. End sentences with the danda '।'. (src: Netflix Hindi; danda per lang:hindi_devanagari)
No italics. Use quotation marks for titles of films, books, albums and programmes: आज मैं थिएटर में "हैमिल्टन" देखने गया था। (src: Netflix Hindi)
Two speakers in one cue: a hyphen with no space before each line (-आओ भी! / -नहीं।). (src: Netflix Hindi)
On-screen text is subtitled only when plot-pertinent, never combined with dialogue in one cue, and shown for as long as the text is on screen. (src: Netflix Hindi)
Use Modern Standard Hindi, not dialect words; bindu may replace chandrabindu for legibility in small type. (src: Netflix Hindi)
Swearing is translated to the same severity and intent, not toned down or up. (src: Netflix Hindi)
mistakes: Break inside a word or a conjunct to make the line fit. Fix: reflow at spaces or cut words.
English words left in Latin in a Hindi cue ('very sorry'). Fix: transliterate: वेरी सॉरी.
'1' and 'एक' mixed in the same file. Fix: the 1-10 words, 11+ digits rule.
A 30-character-per-second cue because the translator kept every word. Fix: condense and check the per-cue rate.
Space before the danda or question mark ('है ।'). Fix: attach punctuation to the last word.
Italics for a film title. Fix: quotation marks.
Dialect or Bhojpuri words in a Hindi cue for a pan-India audience. Fix: standard Hindi, or a note to the client if the dialect is the point.

निकल गया था।

कुछ पता ही नहीं चला।
