-ट्रैकिंग देखो... चार दिन
लगेंगे, ज़्यादा नहीं।

cards.name: Hindi for voice-over and TTS
cards.summary: Write the Hindi script so the engine or the artist says it right the first time: numbers, dates, times, currency, symbols and abbreviations spelled out as Hindi words, English words and brand names in Devanagari, one thought per line, punctuation used as breath marks. A TTS engine reads exactly what is on the page.
use_for: voice-over scripts for reels, explainers, ads and YouTube videos that will be read by a TTS engine or a voice clone
briefing a human voice artist on pronunciation, numbers and pauses
preparing text for SSML-capable engines (say-as, sub, break)
the text-normalisation pass before any Hindi audio is generated
avoid: Sending Roman Hinglish or digits and symbols to a Hindi voice: normalise first.

Using the Mozilla rule 'never transliterate brand names' on a VO script: that rule is for UI text; the script for the voice must be spelled the way it is spoken (the on-screen text can keep the Latin brand).
Trusting one ASR sentence-level read-back as a pass: check word by word (see the local finding below).

sources.title: Raj, Sarkar, Pammi, Yuvaraj, Bansal, Prahallad, Black: Text Processing for Text-to-Speech Systems in Indian Languages (SSW6, 2007)
sources.supports: covers font-to-akshara mapping, pronunciation rules for aksharas, and normalising non-standard words (numbers, abbreviations, dates, currency, addresses) into standard words before synthesis

sources.title: Google Cloud Text-to-Speech: SSML
sources.supports: say-as (cardinal, ordinal, characters, date, currency, telephone, time, fraction), sub alias and break (time or strength) let a script force how a token is read and where pauses fall; the page lists no Hindi-specific caveats, so test each Hindi voice by ear

sources.title: Devanagari Lipi evam Hindi Vartani ka Manakikaran, Central Hindi Directorate, 2024
sources.supports: standard spellings of Hindi number words 1 to 100 (chapter on uniformity of number words) and of ordinals, fractions (डेढ़, ढाई, सवा, साढ़े, पौन) and clock-time phrases (सवा दो बजे, ढाई बजे, पौने तीन बजे); read from a garbled PDF text layer, verify against the print edition

rules: Spell every number as Hindi words in the VO script: 2,500 becomes 'ढाई हज़ार'; 1,500 'डेढ़ हज़ार'; 25 'पच्चीस'; 2026 'दो हज़ार छब्बीस'. Use the standard spellings (CHD): छह, ग्यारह, बाईस, तैंतीस, पैंतालीस, उनतीस, निन्यानवे. Units are हज़ार, लाख, करोड़, अरब. (src: Text Processing for TTS in Indian Languages; CHD 2024 number words)

Fractions and clock times use the spoken forms: डेढ़ (1.5), ढाई (2.5), सवा तीन (3.25), साढ़े तीन (3.5), पौने चार (3.75); 'सवा दो बजे' for 2:15, 'ढाई बजे' for 2:30, 'पौने तीन बजे' for 2:45. (src: CHD 2024)

Dates: write the day as a number word and the month in Devanagari ('पच्चीस अक्टूबर'), and the year as words. Phone numbers: digit by digit with the digit words (शून्य, एक, दो, तीन...), grouped with commas or breaks. (src: normalisation of non-standard words, Text Processing for TTS; the grouping is house practice)

Symbols and abbreviations become the spoken word: ₹ 'रुपये', % 'प्रतिशत', & 'और', 'PM' 'पीएम' or 'प्रधानमंत्री', 'GST' 'जीएसटी', 'UPI' 'यूपीआई', 'Rs' 'रुपये'. Write initialisms as the Devanagari letter names. (src: batch note; Text Processing for TTS)

English words and brand names are written in Devanagari in the VO script ('मोबाइल', 'ऑफ़र', 'स्विगी') because Hindi voices read Roman words with a wrong or letter-by-letter accent; keep the Latin spelling in on-screen text (tech:onscreen_text_vs_vo). Use ऑ for the open o (डॉक्टर). (house practice, unsourced; script rule from lang:hinglish_devanagari)

Use the nuqta on Perso-Arabic sounds you want pronounced (ज़, फ़, क़, ख़, ग़) and write them consistently within the script: it changes pronunciation (सज़ा vs सजा). See lang:urdu_influenced_hindi. (src: Nuqta, Wikipedia, via lang:urdu_influenced_hindi)

Punctuation is the pause: danda '।' or '?' ends a thought, comma gives a short breath, an ellipsis a longer hang. One thought per line, so a line is one breath. Avoid brackets, slashes and em dashes in the spoken text. (house practice, unsourced)

If the engine supports SSML, force readings with say-as (cardinal, ordinal, characters, date, currency, telephone), replace tricky tokens with sub alias, and set pauses with break (for example time='250ms'); then check each Hindi voice by ear because the documentation lists no Hindi-specific behaviour. (src: Google Cloud TTS SSML)

Local test finding, this machine only and not a published source: the F5 Hindi engine tends to drop the first word of a line. This pipeline therefore starts each line with a sacrificial lead word (for example 'हाँ,') and keeps the key word off position one, then verifies the audio word by word with an ASR read-back (faster-whisper). Treat this as engine-specific; other engines differ.
Read the script aloud once before generating; mark every word you stumble on for a respelling or a sub alias. (house practice; see tech:read_aloud)
mistakes: Digits and symbols left in the script ('₹2,500', '25/10'). Fix: normalise to spoken words before synthesis.
Roman Hinglish sent to a Hindi voice, giving a mixed accent. Fix: Devanagari script, Latin only on screen.
'PM' read as letters 'पी एम' by one voice and 'प्रधानमंत्री' by another. Fix: choose the spoken form once and write it out.
The nuqta missing from 'ज़रा', 'फ़र्क़', so the voice says 'जरा', 'फरक'. Fix: add the nuqta where the sound matters, consistently.
A long sentence with three commas read in one breath. Fix: split into short lines and use danda for stops.
ASR read-back at sentence level passes a line whose first word was dropped or doubled, or where नई became नहीं. Fix: word-level read-back on every line (local finding, medium confidence).
Brand name left as 'Swiggy' in the VO text and read letter by letter. Fix: 'स्विगी' in the voice script, 'Swiggy' in the on-screen text.
cards.sample: सुनिए। आज सुबह नौ बजे जयपुर के एक छोटे दफ़्तर में ढाई हज़ार रुपये की रसीद आई। जीएसटी में तीन प्रतिशत का फ़र्क़ निकला। पीएम पोर्टल पर शिकायत करने में सिर्फ़ सवा घंटा लगा। और रिफ़ंड? पच्चीस अक्टूबर तक खाते में आ गया।

cards.name: Everyday Hindustani register (bolchaal Hindi)
cards.summary: The spoken middle register shared by Hindi and Urdu speakers: common words in short, natural sentences, without heavy Sanskrit or Persian-Arabic vocabulary, the language of Bollywood dialogue. It is the default register for Hindi reels, voice-over and social copy.
use_for: Hindi reels, voice-over, ads and captions for a general audience
explainers on money, law, health and government schemes where the reader must understand on first hearing
dialogue for characters and series
rewriting stiff 'shuddh' or translated Hindi into speech
avoid: Using it for devotional, ceremonial or official notices where the tatsam (Sanskrit) word is the expected one: use lang:hindi_devanagari or the devotional card.
Mixing the two directions in one line (heavy Sanskrit next to heavy Persian): keep the register even.
Dialect words, unless a regional flavour is intended (lang:bhojpuri_awadhi_flavour).

sources.title: Hindustani language (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: colloquial Hindustani avoids high-register Sanskrit- or Perso-Arabic-derived words; Bollywood films use this neutral vernacular

rules: Test every content word: would it appear in a Bollywood dialogue or a chat with a friend? If not, swap it for the everyday word. (src: Hindustani language, Wikipedia: colloquial register avoids high-register Sanskrit and Perso-Arabic words)

Everyday swaps: विद्यालय to स्कूल, चिकित्सक to डॉक्टर, अत्यंत to बहुत, आवश्यकता to ज़रूरत, प्रश्न to सवाल, उत्तर to जवाब, सहायता to मदद, समस्या to दिक्कत, आरंभ to शुरू, समाप्त to ख़त्म, पुस्तक to किताब, विवाह to शादी, मित्र to दोस्त, अवश्य to ज़रूर, कठिन to मुश्किल. (general usage; examples are the writer's own)
Use the same everyday word in the other direction too: avoid rare Persian-Arabic words ('तशरीफ़', 'दरख़्वास्त') unless you are writing in the shayari register (lang:urdu_influenced_hindi).
Use contracted, spoken verb forms and short sentences; read each line aloud and cut any sentence that needs a breath in the middle. (house practice; see tech:read_aloud)

Choose the address form by the relationship and keep it for the whole piece: आप for respect, तुम for friends, तू only for close or rough speech. Mixing तुम and आप for one listener reads as an error. (house practice; Mozilla's aap-only rule is for UI, see lang:hindi_devanagari)
Keep English only where speakers use it daily (मोबाइल, ऑफ़र, बैंक, ऐप) and write it in Devanagari (lang:hinglish_devanagari).
Spell by the standard (lang:hindi_devanagari) even in casual copy; informal respellings ('क्यूँ', 'कैसी') belong only in deliberate chat-style dialogue.
mistakes: Translated-from-English stiffness: 'कृपया अपना ओटीपी किसी के साथ साझा न करें'. Fix: 'ओटीपी किसी को मत बताइए।'
Heavy tatsam in a reel hook ('अत्यंत आवश्यक सूचना'). Fix: 'ज़रूरी बात।'
Shayari-level Urdu in a plain explainer ('लम्हा', 'सबब' used five times). Fix: one rare word at most, glossed if kept.
Switching between आप and तुम to the same viewer. Fix: pick one and apply it to verbs and pronouns.
English phrases left in whole clauses inside a Hindi sentence. Fix: swap in single nouns and adjectives only.
cards.sample: भाई, कोई भी फ़ोन करके आपका ओटीपी माँगे, तो सीधा काट दीजिए। बैंक वाले कभी नहीं माँगते। एक बार बता दिया, तो खाता खाली होने में देर नहीं लगती। फ़ोन रखिए, बैंक की ऐप खोलिए, और वहीं से देख लीजिए।

cards.name: Hinglish in Devanagari (English words in Hindi script)
cards.summary: Hindi sentences that keep everyday English words but write them in Devanagari (मोबाइल, डॉक्टर, ऑफ़र). The Hindi grammar frame stays; English nouns and adjectives slot in. It is the script Hindi voices read best and the form Netflix asks for in Hindi dialogue.
use_for: voice-over and TTS scripts for Hindi reels and ads (lang:hindi_voiceover_tts)
Hindi subtitles and captions where English words appear in a Hindi line (lang:hindi_subtitles)
Hindi app, SMS and push copy that mixes familiar English words (ऑफ़र, कैशबैक, ऐप)
newspaper-style Hindi that uses English nouns
avoid: Transliterating whole English clauses: Devanagari English is for single everyday words; longer phrases read badly and TTS mangles them.
Putting Latin words inside a Devanagari sentence meant for a voice: transliterate (brand names stay Latin on screen only).
Using it when the audience reads Roman Hinglish (Instagram captions): that is lang:hinglish_roman.

sources.title: Netflix Hindi Timed Text Style Guide
sources.supports: English words used in a mostly Hindi line of dialogue need no identifiers but should be transliterated into Devanagari with correct spelling (वेरी सॉरी)

sources.title: Devanagari Lipi evam Hindi Vartani ka Manakikaran, Central Hindi Directorate, 2024 edition
sources.supports: standard Devanagari includes the ardhachandra sign ऑ for English sounds: डॉक्टर in the alphabet section, and कॉलेज, हॉल, मॉल, ऑफिस in the spelling rules; foreign words should follow the source language's standard pronunciation as closely as possible. Rules read from a garbled PDF text layer, verify against the print edition

sources.title: Bali et al. 2014, 'I am borrowing ya mixing?' (ACL CodeSwitch workshop)
sources.supports: the common pattern is a Hindi grammatical frame with English words inserted (23.7% of Hindi matrices vs 7.2% the other way); borrowing vs mixing is a continuum

sources.title: Mozilla style guide: Hindi (hi-IN)
sources.supports: brand names are neither translated nor transliterated

rules: Keep a Hindi grammatical frame (verbs, postpositions, word order) and insert English nouns and adjectives into it: 'इस ऑफ़र की वैलिडिटी कल ख़त्म हो रही है'. This is the commonest real-world pattern. (src: Bali et al. 2014)
Write each inserted English word in Devanagari with a correct, consistent spelling: मोबाइल, डॉक्टर, ऑफ़र, स्कूल, स्टेशन, प्लान. No identifier or quotation marks are needed. (src: Netflix Hindi)
Use ऑ (ardhachandra plus आ) for the open 'o' sound of English words: डॉक्टर, कॉलेज, हॉल, मॉल, ऑफ़िस, कॉफ़ी. (src: CHD 2024)

Transliterate close to the English pronunciation, not the English spelling. Write initial clusters directly (स्टेशन, स्कूल), not with a vowel in front (इस्टेशन, इस्कूल). (src: CHD 2024 for pronunciation-based transliteration; the cluster rule is general usage)
Pick one convention for f and z sounds in loanwords and keep it: either nuqta (ऑफ़र, ज़ूम) or none (ऑफर, जूम), across the whole piece. (house practice, unsourced)
Do not double-pluralise: after a number keep the English noun unmarked (तीन ऑफ़र); pick either 'फ़ॉलोअर' or 'फ़ॉलोअर्स' for a series and keep it. (house practice, unsourced)
Brand names stay in Latin in on-screen and UI text (Mozilla hi-IN rule), and are transliterated only in the voice-over script (see lang:hindi_voiceover_tts). (src: Mozilla hi-IN)
Use Latin digits and keep an acronym in Latin in on-screen text (UPI, GST); spell it as Devanagari letters in the voice-over script. (house practice; see lang:hindi_voiceover_tts)
mistakes: 'डाक्टर' or 'आफिस' with a plain आ. Fix: ऑ, as in डॉक्टर and ऑफ़िस.
A whole English clause transliterated ('आई विल कॉल यू लेटर'). Fix: write the clause in Hindi.
Latin and Devanagari mixed inside one word ('मobile'). Fix: one script per word.
Inconsistent spellings across a project (ऑफ़र / ऑफर / ओफर). Fix: one entry in the style sheet.
Roman Hinglish pasted into a Hindi TTS tool. Fix: transliterate to Devanagari first.
A brand name transliterated in a UI string. Fix: keep the Latin name; transliterate only for the voice.
cards.sample: इस बार का ऑफ़र सच में अलग है। मोबाइल रिचार्ज पर कैशबैक सीधा आपके वॉलेट में आएगा, और वैलिडिटी भी पूरे तीस दिन की है। बस ऐप खोलिए, ऑफ़र सेक्शन में जाइए और एक टैप में एक्टिवेट कीजिए।

cards.name: Hinglish in Roman script
cards.summary: Hindi-English code-mixing typed in Latin letters, the script most Hindi speakers use online. There is no standard spelling, so the craft is choosing one spelling per word the way the audience types it, and keeping to it across the whole series.
use_for: Instagram and YouTube captions, comments, replies and hashtags for Hindi-speaking audiences
WhatsApp broadcasts, SMS and push copy in a casual voice
on-screen text and hook lines on reels where the audience reads Roman letters
creator, D2C and fintech brand voice for urban north India
avoid: Feeding Roman Hinglish to a Hindi voice or TTS engine: give it Devanagari (lang:hinglish_devanagari, lang:hindi_voiceover_tts).
Scholarly diacritics (ā, ṭ): informal spelling only (lang:hindi_romanisation_schemes).
Formal documents, legal notices and government-style copy: use lang:hindi_devanagari or English.

sources.title: Hinglish (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: Hinglish = code-switching between colloquial Hindi and English, in writing usually Romanised; a cited YouTube-comment study found Romanised Hindi (52% of comments) far ahead of Devanagari (1%); Google added Romanised Hindi support to Gboard, Search and Google Pay; dominant in urban northern India, Bollywood, advertising and social media

rules: Pick one spelling per word and keep it for the whole series: hai (not he/hae), hain, nahi (or nahin: choose), kya, kyun, bahut, mein, aur, toh. Keep the list in the style sheet (edit:style_sheet). (src: batch note; Hinglish, Wikipedia: no standard spelling)

Spell for how the audience types, not how a scheme prescribes: no diacritics, no 'aa/ee' stretching in headlines ('pyar', not 'pyaaar') unless a deliberate emphasis that you use once per post. (house practice, unsourced)
Write the English word in its English spelling ('office', 'offer', 'cashback') and the Hindi word in the typed spelling; never respell English words phonetically ('ofis'). (house practice, unsourced)

Keep the Hindi grammar frame and insert English nouns and adjectives; the commonest natural pattern is Hindi sentence with English words, not the reverse (see Bali et al. 2014 on lang:hinglish_devanagari). (src: Bali et al. 2014, via lang:hinglish_devanagari)
One address form per piece: aap, tum or tu, matched to the brand tone; do not mix 'tum' and 'aap' for the same reader. (house practice, unsourced)

Use Latin punctuation: '.', '?', '!' and comma; the danda is for Devanagari text only. Use Latin digits and lakh/crore for rupee amounts (lang:india_locale_formats). (house practice; Mozilla hi-IN for digits)

For on-screen text, treat it as Latin-script text and keep to short lines, up to two lines of about 42 characters, as in lang:english_subtitles. (house practice; the 42-character figure is Netflix's English line limit)

Check search spelling before you finalise a keyword-bearing line: type the first letters in Search or Gboard and use the spelling that autocomplete offers (lang:hindi_seo). (src: Hinglish, Wikipedia, for Google's Roman Hindi support)
If a caption is also voiced, keep a parallel Devanagari script for the voice (lang:hindi_voiceover_tts). (house practice)
mistakes: 'Nahi', 'nahin', 'nai' and 'nhi' in one series. Fix: one house spelling, enforced by search-and-replace before posting.
Phonetic English ('ofis', 'mobail'). Fix: English words in English spelling.
Drawn-out spellings used in every line ('kyaaa baat haiii'), which read as noise. Fix: stretch one word per post at most, for emphasis.
Switching between tum and aap for the same person. Fix: pick one in the voice guide.
A Devanagari danda in a Roman caption. Fix: use a Latin full stop.
Treating the 52% / 1% YouTube-comment figure as a measure of all Indian users. Fix: say 'one study of YouTube comments found...' or leave it out.
cards.sample: Monday ka mood off hai? Chalo ek kaam karte hain: 10 minute ka walk, ek cutting chai aur phone ko drawer mein band. Sach bol raha hoon, dimaag ghar wapas aa jaata hai. Aaj try karo aur comment mein batao, kitne baje tak phone se door reh paaye.

cards.name: Indian number, currency and date formats
cards.summary: Lakh and crore with 2-digit grouping after the first three digits (12,34,56,789), the rupee sign U+20B9, and day-month-year dates, for Indian readers in English, Hindi and Hinglish. Choose lakh/crore or million/billion once per piece, and show both when the reader might be global.
use_for: any copy with rupee amounts, populations, budgets, revenues or scheme outlays
news, finance, fintech, government and real-estate writing for Indian readers
converting an Indian figure for a global reader and the reverse
dates and times in notices, emails and UI strings
avoid: Western grouping for rupee amounts (1,500,000 for 15 lakh) in India-facing copy.
Lakh and crore in a piece for a global audience without a conversion on first use.
Hybrids such as 'Rs 10 lakhs crore': use 'lakh crore' as one fixed unit.

sources.title: Indian numbering system (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: lakh = 100,000, crore = 10 million; digits grouped in pairs after the first three (123,456,789 is 12,34,56,789); both 'lakh' and 'lakhs' are used in Indian English; 1 lakh crore = 10^12; Indian publications use lakh/crore for rupee amounts and international units for foreign currency; en-IN and hi-IN locales are supported in Unicode CLDR

sources.title: Best Practices for Localisation of e-Governance Applications in Indian Languages, v5.7 (Govt of India, L10N-eGov, Jan 2014)
sources.supports: rupee sign must be stored as U+20B9; India date shown as DD-MM-YY; English (Latin) digits recommended where numbers are computed

sources.title: Mozilla style guide: Hindi (hi-IN)
sources.supports: Hindi dates written day-month-year with the month in Devanagari (25 सितम्बर 2016); times with a colon (10:30 बजे); Latin digits

rules: Units: 1 lakh = 1,00,000 (100,000); 1 crore = 1,00,00,000 (10 million); 1 lakh crore = 10^12. (src: Indian numbering system, Wikipedia)

Grouping: the first three digits from the right form a group, then pairs: 123,456,789 is written 12,34,56,789; 500,000 is 5,00,000. When code produces numbers, use the en-IN or hi-IN locale (Unicode CLDR) instead of hand-grouping. (src: Indian numbering system, Wikipedia)

Rupee amounts for Indian readers use lakh and crore; foreign-currency amounts use international units (million, billion). Do not write a dollar figure in crore. (src: Indian numbering system, Wikipedia)
Choose 'lakh' or 'lakhs' once and keep it; both are used in Indian English. 'Lakh crore' never takes an s on lakh. (src: Indian numbering system, Wikipedia; choose-one is house practice)
For a global reader, give the plain conversion on first use: '₹120 crore (1.2 billion rupees)'. Conversions: 10 lakh = 1 million; 100 crore = 1 billion. (src: Indian numbering system, Wikipedia)

The rupee sign is ₹ (U+20B9); do not use an image or a look-alike letter. Choose one form per piece: ₹, Rs or INR, not a mix. (src: e-Governance localisation best practices; one-form rule is house practice)

Dates are day-month-year. In English write '5 October 2026' with the month as a word so a global reader cannot read 05/10 as May. In forms and tables the Indian numeric order is DD-MM-YY. (src: e-Governance localisation best practices; month-as-word is house practice)
In Hindi write the date with the month in Devanagari ('25 सितम्बर 2026') and the time with a colon ('10:30 बजे'). (src: Mozilla hi-IN)
Use Latin digits 0-9 in Hindi and Hinglish copy and wherever a number is computed. (src: e-Governance localisation best practices; Mozilla hi-IN)
For voice-over, write the amount as Hindi words (ढाई हज़ार रुपये, तीन करोड़), see lang:hindi_voiceover_tts. (src: CHD 2024 via lang:hindi_voiceover_tts)
mistakes: '₹1,500,000' for a 15 lakh price on an Indian page. Fix: ₹15,00,000 or ₹15 lakh.
'₹10 lakhs crore'. Fix: ₹10 lakh crore.
'$5 crore' or '₹1.2 billion' in an India-facing news piece. Fix: $50 million (foreign currency, international units); ₹120 crore for rupees.
'03/04/2026' on a page read by Indian and US readers. Fix: '3 April 2026'.
'Rs. 500', '₹500' and 'INR 500' in one email. Fix: choose one.
Revenue given in crore with no conversion in an investor deck for foreign funds. Fix: add the million/billion figure on first use.
cards.sample: Our Pune factory crossed ₹120 crore in revenue for FY 2025-26, up from ₹96 crore the year before. The new plant at Chakan, which cost ₹18.5 crore, opens on 14 November 2026. For overseas readers: ₹120 crore is 1.2 billion rupees.

cards.name: Indian English
cards.summary: British-based spelling with -ise, lakh and crore for rupee amounts, and a set of India-specific words and habits (prepone, do the needful, out of station, plural 'equipments') that Indian readers understand and global readers often do not. Write it fully for India-only audiences and clean it for global ones.
use_for: emails, web copy, press notes and ads for Indian readers
Indian clients' brand and corporate writing in English
editing English drafted by Indian writers for a global or US/UK client
deciding when an Indianism is a voice choice and when it is a mistake
avoid: Indianisms in copy for global readers: swap them (see the mistakes list) or move to lang:global_plain_english.
Mixing American spellings into British-spelt Indian copy (and the reverse) inside one piece.
Overplaying 'Hinglish English' for comedy in a corporate or legal context.

sources.title: Indian English (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: follows British spelling (travelling, litre, practise as a verb, anaesthesia, fulfil, catalogue, realise, colour); lakh/crore in formal publications; Indianisms such as prepone, do the needful, pass out (graduate), out of station, revert (reply with information), kindly adjust, hotel for a restaurant, emphatic 'only'; mass nouns such as equipment, evidence, training treated as count nouns

sources.title: American and British English spelling differences (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: India follows British usage; India strongly prefers -ise over -ize

rules: Spelling is British: colour, centre, organise, realise, travelling, catalogue, fulfil, anaesthesia; practice (noun) but practise (verb); litre. India strongly prefers -ise to -ize, so default to -ise. (src: Indian English and American and British spelling differences, Wikipedia)
Money and large numbers use lakh and crore with Indian grouping for rupees (₹4,50,000 or ₹4.5 lakh); see lang:india_locale_formats. (src: Indian English, Wikipedia)
Dates are day-month-year ('16 October 2026'); no comma after the month. (house practice: the Indian English article gives no date format; day-month-year is the British-Indian order)

Know the Indianisms and decide on purpose: 'prepone' (move earlier), 'do the needful' (take the necessary action), 'pass out' (graduate), 'out of station' (away from the city), 'revert' (reply with information), 'kindly adjust' (please bear with the inconvenience), 'hotel' (a restaurant or cafe), emphatic 'only' ('I live here only'). (src: Indian English, Wikipedia)
For India-only audiences these are understood; keep them out of contracts, formal notices and anything a global reader or translator will see. (house practice, unsourced)

Treat mass nouns as uncountable in anything formal: equipment, evidence, training, information, advice. Write 'items of equipment' or 'training sessions', not 'equipments' or 'trainings'. (src: Indian English, Wikipedia, for the habit; the fix is house practice)
Choose 'please reply' where you mean reply: 'revert' can read as 'go back to the earlier state' to a global reader. (house practice, unsourced)
Use the client's own house style if it exists; record the choice (spelling set, date order, Oxford comma) in the style sheet. (edit:style_sheet)
mistakes: 'Please prepone the meeting' in an email to a London client. Fix: 'Can we move the meeting earlier?'
'Kindly do the needful' as a closing line. Fix: say exactly what you need and by when.
'We have many equipments and trainings.' Fix: 'We have a lot of equipment and run many training sessions.'
'Passed out from IIT in 2019' in global copy. Fix: 'graduated from IIT in 2019'.
'I am out of station till Monday' to a client who may not know the idiom. Fix: 'I am away until Monday'.
Mixed '-ise' and '-ize' in one document. Fix: one rule (-ise) and a check pass.
'Hotel' in a restaurant guide for visitors from abroad. Fix: 'restaurant'.
cards.sample: Hi Meera, the festival-season catalogue is ready for your review. We have kept prices in rupees (₹4,999 to ₹24,999) and used 'colour' and 'organise' throughout, as agreed. Could you reply by Friday, 16 October 2026? If the dates need to move earlier, tell us and we will bring them forward. The equipment photos are attached.

cards.name: Localisation QA
cards.summary: Check translated or transcreated copy against an error typology before it ships: terminology, accuracy, linguistic conventions, style, locale conventions, audience appropriateness and design/markup (MQM's seven dimensions), plus script checks for Indic text. Native readers do the final pass, in the real layout.
use_for: reviewing Hindi, Hinglish and regional-language versions of ads, UI, subtitles and documents
signing off an agency or vendor's translation before it goes to a client
setting a pre-publish checklist for multilingual content
writing review comments that separate meaning errors from taste
avoid: A spelling-and-grammar pass alone: it misses wrong numbers, wrong locale formats and broken layout.
Reviewing in a document file when the copy ships in a button, image or video: check in the final layout.
Using it as a substitute for a native reader's judgment on tone and audience fit.

sources.title: MQM (Multidimensional Quality Metrics) error typology
sources.supports: seven top-level dimensions: terminology, accuracy, linguistic conventions, style, locale conventions, audience appropriateness, design and markup; MQM Core vs Full

sources.title: Best Practices for Localisation of e-Governance Applications in Indian Languages, v5.7 (Govt of India, Jan 2014)
sources.supports: Unicode storage, rupee sign U+20B9, locale date format, Latin digits for computed numbers, avoid slang and disputed maps in source content

sources.title: Mozilla style guide: Hindi (hi-IN)
sources.supports: never translate variables, placeholders or tags (%ld, HTML tags); danda not pipe; Latin digits; keep the target text from growing far beyond the source

rules: Sort every finding under one MQM dimension: terminology, accuracy, linguistic conventions (grammar, spelling, punctuation), style, locale conventions (number, currency, date and time formats), audience appropriateness, design and markup. (src: MQM typology)

Run automated checks first: placeholders and tags unchanged (never translate variables like %ld or HTML tags), numbers and dates match the source, terminology list applied. (src: Mozilla hi-IN; MQM typology)

Then a bilingual read against the source for accuracy (mistranslation, omission, addition), then a monolingual read of the target by a native reader for fluency and tone. (house practice; MQM accuracy and style dimensions)

Check locale conventions: rupee sign U+20B9, lakh/crore grouping for rupees, day-month-year dates, Latin digits where numbers are computed. (src: e-Governance localisation best practices; lang:india_locale_formats)

Script checks for Indic text: the danda is U+0964 (not '|', 'l' or 'I'); matras and conjuncts render correctly in the target font with no broken ligatures or missing-glyph boxes; nuqta used consistently and the file normalised to NFC; no Latin look-alike characters or stray Latin digits. (src: Mozilla hi-IN for danda and digits; the other script checks are house practice)
Check slang, idioms and sensitive content: avoid slang that does not translate, and check disputed maps and borders in images and infographics. (src: e-Governance localisation best practices)

Check design and markup in the real layout: text not truncated or overflowing, line breaks not splitting words, correct font in every script (Urdu right-to-left). (src: MQM design and markup dimension; Urdu RTL is general usage)
Check audience appropriateness: references, festivals, colours, gestures and humour suit the locale and the segment. (src: MQM audience appropriateness dimension)
Return findings with the dimension, the exact location, the fix and a priority; meaning, legal and offensive errors first. (house practice, unsourced)
mistakes: Spell-check only. Fix: run all seven dimensions, at least automated plus one native read.
Price '1,500,000' left in a Hindi page for ₹15,00,000. Fix: locale-format check.
A pipe '|' typed for the danda throughout a Hindi file. Fix: global replace to U+0964, then check.
Translated placeholder '%s' or '{name}' broke the sentence. Fix: automated placeholder diff.
Hindi text in a button that overflows and wraps mid-word. Fix: review in the layout and shorten.
A map with a disputed border used in a regional version. Fix: use the client-approved map.
The same term translated three ways across a campaign. Fix: terminology list applied and checked.
cards.sample:
QA log, Hindi landing page
1 | Locale conventions | Price shows 1,500,000, should read 15,00,000 | fix
2 | Linguistic conventions | Danda typed as a pipe in the footer | fix
3 | Accuracy | 'free delivery above ₹999' became 'ऑफ़र 999 रुपये': drop the condition | critical
4 | Design | CTA button text wraps to a second line at 360 px width | fix

cards.name: Regional Indian languages (overview)
cards.summary: India's next-largest languages after Hindi (Bengali, Marathi, Telugu, Tamil, Gujarati, Urdu, Kannada, Odia, Malayalam, Punjabi), each with its own script and writing conventions. Content for them is transcreated by a native writer from the brief or the English source, never run through Hindi.
use_for: deciding which language and script to add after Hindi for a campaign or product
briefing native writers and reviewers for regional versions
setting script, font and layout checks for each language before production
sizing the regional opportunity with sourced Census 2011 and IAMAI figures
avoid: Hindi-to-regional relay translation: brief the native writer from the English source and the creative intent.
Passing Hindi off as Marathi: both use Devanagari, but spelling and vocabulary differ.
Writing per-language style rules from memory: this card gives scripts and audience sizes only; the writing rules belong to a native reviewer.

sources.title: Languages of India (Wikipedia, Census 2011 table)
sources.supports: first-language speakers 2011: Bengali 97.2M (Bengali script), Marathi 83.0M (Devanagari), Telugu 81.1M, Tamil 69.0M, Gujarati 55.5M, Urdu 50.8M (Perso-Arabic), Kannada 43.7M, Odia 37.5M, Malayalam 34.8M, Punjabi 33.1M (Gurmukhi); 22 Eighth Schedule languages

sources.title: IAMAI and Kantar, Internet in India 2024
sources.supports: 98% of internet users accessed Indic-language content in 2024; urban preference split by language is charted

sources.title: Best Practices for Localisation of e-Governance Applications in Indian Languages, v5.7
sources.supports: 22 official languages and 12 scripts; Unicode and CLDR locale data per language

rules: Use the Census 2011 first-language counts to rank languages: Bengali 97.2M, Marathi 83.0M, Telugu 81.1M, Tamil 69.0M, Gujarati 55.5M, Urdu 50.8M, Kannada 43.7M, Odia 37.5M, Malayalam 34.8M, Punjabi 33.1M. They are 2011 counts, not today's; say so. (src: Languages of India, Wikipedia)

Scripts: Bengali in Bengali script, Marathi in Devanagari, Urdu in Perso-Arabic script (written right to left), Punjabi in Gurmukhi; Telugu, Tamil, Gujarati, Kannada, Odia and Malayalam each in their own script. India has 22 Eighth Schedule languages and 12 scripts. (src: Languages of India, Wikipedia; e-Governance localisation best practices)
Brief a native writer for each language from the creative intent and the English or source text; do not translate through Hindi. (house practice; see lang:transcreation)
Marathi shares Devanagari with Hindi but not its spelling or vocabulary: never reuse Hindi copy as Marathi. (src: batch note; Languages of India, Wikipedia, for the script)

Production checks per language: Unicode storage, a font that covers the script, correct rendering of conjuncts and matras, Latin digits for computed numbers, and right-to-left layout for Urdu. (src: e-Governance localisation best practices; RTL is general usage)
Run lang:localization_qa on every version with a reader who speaks the language natively; keep one named reviewer per language. (house practice)
Size the demand with IAMAI-Kantar: 98% of internet users accessed Indic-language content in 2024. Write 'Indic-language content', not 'regional content', when you cite it. (src: IAMAI-Kantar 2024)
mistakes: Marathi page built by lightly editing the Hindi one. Fix: a Marathi writer rewrites from the brief.
A Tamil or Telugu version translated from the Hindi script, carrying Hindi idioms. Fix: transcreate from the source.
Urdu text pasted into a left-to-right layout so punctuation lands on the wrong side. Fix: set the container to RTL and review a screenshot.
Font fallback replaces Odia or Kannada letters with boxes. Fix: embed a covering font and test on a real phone.
Using 2011 speaker counts as if current. Fix: label the year and the source.
One creative for every language with only the text swapped, so imagery clashes with the market. Fix: transcreate the visuals and references too.
cards.sample: Brief to a Marathi transcreation writer: 'Our Pune bakery's Diwali box is for families who open the box together. Keep that moment: warm, a little teasing, no sales shout. Do not translate the English line below; write one Marathi headline and one Hinglish-free CTA that fit a 1080x1350 post.'

cards.name: Sanskrit shlokas in devotional content (Devanagari + IAST)
cards.summary: Quote shlokas in Devanagari with the danda and double danda as the only verse punctuation and, when a Roman line is needed, lossless IAST diacritics. A shloka is copied from a reliable edition with its source reference, because a single wrong matra changes the meaning.
use_for: devotional reels, carousels and captions that show a verse (aarti, stotra, gita, upanishad lines)
educational posts that explain a shloka word by word
scholarly or reference lines in blog posts, books and show notes
subtitle and voice-over scripts for devotional content (genre:devotional_content)
avoid: Retyping a shloka from memory or from a social post: copy it from a reliable edition and cite chapter and verse.
IAST on a reel screen: show the Devanagari plus a plain Hindi or English meaning; keep IAST for notes and references.
Adding commas, full stops or quotation marks inside the verse: Sanskrit verse uses only the danda and double danda.

sources.title: International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: IAST is a lossless romanisation: macrons for long vowels, underdots for retroflexes, ś ṣ ṃ ḥ ṅ ñ; ISO 15919 follows it closely (r̥ for vocalic r; ē ō); capitals allowed on proper names; standard in scholarly publishing

sources.title: Danda (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: in Sanskrit, danda and double danda are the only punctuation: double danda closes a verse, single danda a half-verse

sources.title: Devanagari Lipi evam Hindi Vartani ka Manakikaran, Central Hindi Directorate, 2024
sources.supports: Sanskrit conventions inside the Hindi standard: halant kept in Sanskrit indeclinables (अर्थात्, पश्चात्); avagraha ऽ (सोऽहं); visarga ः written attached to the letter, unlike the colon sign. Read from a garbled PDF text layer, verify against the print edition

rules: Master text is Devanagari, copied from a reliable printed or critical edition; add the source and the chapter and verse (for example 'Bhagavad Gita 2.47'). A single wrong matra or conjunct changes the meaning. (src: batch note; house practice)

Verse punctuation is the danda ('।', U+0964) after a half-verse and the double danda ('॥', U+0965) at the end of the verse; no commas, full stops or quotation marks inside the verse. (src: Danda, Wikipedia)

Set the verse one half-verse per line and keep each danda on the same line as its last word (use a no-break space before it); place the verse reference after the closing double danda. (house practice, unsourced)
Keep the Sanskrit forms: the halant at the end of indeclinables (अर्थात्, पश्चात्), the avagraha ऽ (सोऽहं), and the visarga ः attached to the letter (not a typed colon ':'). (src: CHD 2024)

Romanise with IAST for any reference line: long vowels ā ī ū, retroflexes ṭ ḍ ṇ ṣ, vocalic ṛ, and ś ṃ ḥ ṅ ñ. Use ISO 15919 only when one scheme must cover several Indian scripts (it writes r̥, ē, ō). (src: IAST, Wikipedia)

IAST allows capitals on proper names (Kṛṣṇa, Rāma); keep the verse itself in lower case. Type precomposed letters (ā, ṣ, ṭ), choose a font that has the Latin Extended Additional block, and check that no letter turns into a box. (src: IAST, Wikipedia, for capitalisation; font note is house practice)
For a reel or carousel: show the Devanagari and one plain meaning line in Hindi or English; put the IAST and the source in the caption or show notes. (src: batch note)

For voice-over, give the engine the Devanagari verse with the sandhi as printed, and have a person who knows the verse listen to the output; a TTS tuned for Hindi often mispronounces Sanskrit. (house practice, unsourced)
Write your own translation as a paraphrase and say so; do not paste a published translation without credit. (house practice; copyright)
mistakes: Verse copied from a reel's caption with a wrong matra. Fix: copy from a reliable edition and keep the edition in the notes.
A comma after each pada, or a full stop at the end, in the verse. Fix: danda and double danda only.
Colon typed for the visarga ('दुःखभाग' written 'दुः खभाग'). Fix: the visarga attached to the letter.
Hunterian-style romanisation ('pashyantu', 'shloka') in a reference line, losing ś and ṣ. Fix: IAST (śloka, paśyantu).
IAST on the reel screen where most viewers read Devanagari or Roman Hindi. Fix: Devanagari plus meaning on screen; IAST in the caption.
No source given for the verse. Fix: add chapter and verse or the text name.
Danda wrapped to the start of the next line. Fix: no-break space before the danda.
cards.sample:
सर्वे भवन्तु सुखिनः सर्वे सन्तु निरामयाः ।
सर्वे भद्राणि पश्यन्तु मा कश्चिद्दुःखभाग्भवेत् ॥

sarve bhavantu sukhinaḥ sarve santu nirāmayāḥ |
sarve bhadrāṇi paśyantu mā kaścid duḥkhabhāg bhavet ||

Meaning: May everyone be happy and free of illness; may everyone see what is good; may no one suffer.

cards.name: Transcreation (vs translation)
cards.summary: Recreate the message for a new language and culture so it lands with the same intent, tone and emotion, changing words, references and imagery as needed. Hooks, puns, rhymes and CTAs are transcreated; legal text, specifications and prices are translated literally and then reviewed.
use_for: taglines, hooks, ad copy and campaign themes moving from English to Hindi, Hinglish or a regional language
adapting a global campaign for India (references, festivals, imagery, humour)
briefing and reviewing a native writer on creative localisation
choosing where literal translation is enough and where it is not
avoid: Using it for legal, regulatory, price and specification text: translate those literally and have them reviewed.
Erasing the brand: keep the brand name and the approved brand elements; change the expression, not the identity.
Skipping a back-translation: the client must be able to see what the new line means.

sources.title: Transcreation (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: keeps intent, style, tone and context; adapts imagery and culture; used in marketing, ads, games; Spider-Man: India as an example

sources.title: Microsoft Style Guide: Global communications
sources.supports: translation changes the language; localization adapts content to a locale's language, cultural and political expectations and is done by people who know that culture

sources.title: KPMG and Google, Indian Languages: Defining India's Internet (April 2017)
sources.supports: Indian-language users show higher propensity to respond to digital ads in their own language and see local-language content as more reliable

rules: Start from intent, not words: write a one-paragraph brief with the audience, the feeling the line must create, the action it must trigger and what may change (words, references, imagery, humour) and what may not (brand name, legal claims). (house practice; src: Transcreation, Wikipedia: keeps intent, style, tone, context)

Sort the source line by line: literal translation for legal text, specifications, prices and instructions; transcreation for hooks, puns, rhymes, idioms and CTAs. (src: batch note; Microsoft translation vs localization)
Give the writer the source text and the creative intent; give the reviewer a back-translation into English of each option so the client can approve what the line means. (house practice, unsourced)

Replace references that exist only in the source culture (a sport, festival, food, celebrity or idiom) with a local equivalent, or drop them; adapt imagery and examples the same way. (src: Transcreation, Wikipedia: adapts imagery and culture)
Use a native writer of the target language and locale; localisation is done by people who know the culture. (src: Microsoft global communications)
Offer two or three options for headlines and taglines, each with a one-line rationale. (house practice, unsourced)
Check the transcreated line against length and layout limits (subtitles, buttons, banners), then run lang:localization_qa. (house practice)

Why it pays: Indian-language users respond more to digital ads in their own language and see local-language content as more reliable; use this as the argument, citing KPMG-Google 2017, and do not attach a percentage the source does not give. (src: KPMG-Google 2017)
A famous example to point to, by name only: the Spider-Man: India adaptation. (src: Transcreation, Wikipedia)
mistakes: Literal translation of a pun or idiom. Fix: find the target-language equivalent or build a new line with the same effect.
A cricket or baseball metaphor kept in a language market that does not use it. Fix: local reference or plain wording.
Transcreating the terms and conditions as if they were a hook. Fix: literal translation plus legal review.
No back-translation, so the client approves a line they cannot read. Fix: attach the back-translation.
Translating the brand name or tagline against brand rules (Mozilla hi-IN: brand names are not localised). Fix: follow the brand sheet.
Using Hindi as a bridge for a Tamil or Bengali version. Fix: brief a native writer from the source.
cards.sample:
Source (English, CA firm, Jaipur): 'Start the new financial year with a clean slate.'
Transcreation (Hinglish): 'Naya saal, purana hisaab saaf. Pehle GST ka jhanjhat nipta lo.'
Note: 'clean slate' is not used literally; 'hisaab saaf' is how an Indian accountant would say it.

cards.name: UK English
cards.summary: British spelling and conventions: -our, -ise (or Oxford -ize), -re, doubled l (travelled), licence and practice as nouns against license and practise as verbs, programme for non-computing uses, and day-month-year dates. Commonwealth countries normally follow British usage; pick one house setting and apply it throughout.
use_for: copy for UK, Irish and most Commonwealth clients
Indian clients who want British spelling (see lang:indian_english)
documents that follow a UK style guide or UK regulator
proofreading a draft that mixes British and American spellings
avoid: Mixing UK and US spelling in one piece (a UK -our beside a US -er).
Treating -ize as an error: Oxford spelling is a valid British house style; pick -ise or -ize on purpose.
Using it for US-market copy (lang:us_english).

sources.title: American and British English spelling differences (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: British patterns: colour, organise (or Oxford organize), centre, travelled, licence/license and practice/practise noun-verb split, defence, anaemia, programme, cheque, tyre, grey, plough, ageing; Oxford spelling keeps -ize; Commonwealth countries normally follow British usage

rules: -our: colour, labour, honour, favour. (src: spelling differences, Wikipedia)

-ise as the default: organise, realise, recognise; or Oxford spelling, which keeps -ize (organize, realize) with every other British form. Choose one and apply it to the whole piece. (src: spelling differences, Wikipedia)
-re: centre, theatre, metre, calibre. (src: spelling differences, Wikipedia)
Doubled consonant before -ed/-ing: travelled, cancelled, labelled, modelling. (src: spelling differences, Wikipedia)
Noun and verb split: licence (noun) / license (verb); practice (noun) / practise (verb). 'Defence' takes -ce. (src: spelling differences, Wikipedia)

Other British forms: catalogue, dialogue, anaemia, oestrogen, paediatrician, programme (for a scheme or event; 'program' for computing), cheque, tyre, grey, plough, ageing. (src: spelling differences, Wikipedia)
Dates are day-month-year ('5 October 2026'), and single quotation marks are the usual UK choice for quotes, with double marks inside. Check the client's house style. (house practice, unsourced)
Set the proofing language of your tool to English (UK) and read the final file once for stray American forms. (house practice, unsourced)
Record the choices (-ise or -ize, quote style, Oxford comma) in the style sheet so later pieces match. (edit:style_sheet)
mistakes: 'Colour' and 'center' in the same page. Fix: apply -re everywhere.
'License' used as a noun ('a valid license'). Fix: 'licence' for the noun, 'license' for the verb.
'Practice' used as a verb ('practice daily'). Fix: 'practise'.
'Travelled' beside 'traveling'. Fix: doubled l in every form.
Replacing every -ize with -ise in a client text that uses Oxford spelling. Fix: ask which house style it uses.
Spell-checker left on US English, silently Americanising. Fix: switch the proofing language.
cards.sample: Our travelling team will organise a free demonstration at the centre on 14 November, with the licence paperwork ready for inspection. Practise at home beforehand. We have cancelled the earlier session and labelled the new rooms by colour, so you can find your way easily.

cards.name: Urdu-influenced Hindi (shayari register, nuqta)
cards.summary: Hindi coloured with Perso-Arabic vocabulary for shayari, romance and poetic captions, with nuqta letters (क़ ख़ ग़ ज़ फ़) marking the borrowed sounds. The craft is placing the nuqta only where the sound is spoken and being consistent, since it is optional in Hindi, changes meaning in some pairs and changes TTS pronunciation.
use_for: shayari, ghazal-style couplets, romantic and nostalgic captions (genre:shayari)
film-song style lyrics and voice-over with an Urdu feel
heritage, Mughal-era and Lucknowi cultural writing where the vocabulary is part of the subject
checking nuqta use in any Hindi text read aloud (lang:hindi_voiceover_tts)
avoid: Heavy Urdu vocabulary in plain explainers: use lang:hindustani_everyday and gloss any rare word.
Treating Perso-Arabic vocabulary as a religious marker in political, satirical or character copy: it is a register, not an identity label.
Putting nuqta on Hindi or Sanskrit words (जल, फल, फूल, गंगा): that is over-correction.

sources.title: Nuqta (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: nuqta (U+093C) marks Perso-Arabic sounds in Devanagari (क़ qilā, ख़ khān, ग़ kāġaz, ज़ z, फ़ f); its use in Hindi is optional and inconsistent; precomposed nuqta letters U+0958-095F exist and decompose under NFC; it separates pairs such as सज़ा/सजा, ज़हर/जहर; ड़ and ढ़ are Hindi flap sounds written with it

sources.title: Hindustani language (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: Urdu register draws on Persian and Arabic vocabulary; grammar is shared with Hindi

sources.title: Devanagari Lipi evam Hindi Vartani ka Manakikaran, Central Hindi Directorate, 2024
sources.supports: nuqta is not in the core Hindi alphabet; Urdu words that Hindi has absorbed (कलम, किला, दाग) are written in Hindi form without nuqta; nuqta continues in transliteration of Urdu texts. Read from a garbled PDF text layer, verify against the print edition

sources.title: Netflix Hindi Timed Text Style Guide
sources.supports: example line with nuqta: मेरी ग़लती है

rules: Nuqta letters and sounds: क़ (q), ख़ (x, a throat sound), ग़ (gh), ज़ (z), फ़ (f). ड़ and ढ़ (flap sounds) also carry it but are Hindi sounds and are always written with it: बड़ा, पढ़ना. (src: Nuqta, Wikipedia)

Use the nuqta on Perso-Arabic words where the sound is spoken: ज़िंदगी, ग़म, ख़ुशी, इश्क़, वक़्त, ख़्वाब, ज़रा, फ़ासला, क़सम, ग़ज़ल, ख़ामोशी, ज़ख़्म. Do not add it to Hindi or Sanskrit words: जल, फल, फूल, गंगा. (src: Nuqta, Wikipedia for the letters; the word list is the writer's own)

Be consistent: the nuqta is optional in Hindi, so decide per project whether you write it on every Perso-Arabic word (shayari, lyrics, subtitles, voice-over) or follow the Central Hindi Directorate's practice of dropping it on absorbed words (कलम, किला, दाग) and keeping it only for Urdu transliteration. Do not mix within a piece. (src: Nuqta, Wikipedia; CHD 2024)

It changes meaning in some pairs: सज़ा (punishment) / सजा (decorated), राज़ (secret) / राज (rule), ज़ीना (stairs) / जीना (to live), ख़ुदा (God) / खुदा (dug). (src: Nuqta, Wikipedia, for सज़ा/सजा and the principle; other pairs are standard usage)

Encoding: type the letter as base + nuqta (U+093C) or as the precomposed letters (U+0958-U+095F), and normalise the finished file to NFC; precomposed letters decompose under NFC, so a mixed file looks identical but searches and diffs disagree until you normalise. (src: Nuqta, Wikipedia)
Izafat links are written with hyphens on both sides: दर्द-ए-दिल, शाम-ओ-सहर. (general usage, unsourced)
Gloss a rare word in a short line below the couplet ('मतलब: ...') and keep the vocabulary level even; one very rare word per couplet is enough. (house practice, unsourced)
For voice-over, keep the nuqta on every Perso-Arabic word so the engine or artist says z, f, q, gh correctly. (src: batch note; lang:hindi_voiceover_tts)

The Central Hindi Directorate's 2024 spelling standard treats the nukta as outside the standard Hindi alphabet and does not use it on absorbed Urdu words (कलम, किला, दाग); it keeps it only when transliterating Urdu text. Use that for formal / government Hindi; keep the nukta in shayari, lyrics and voice-over scripts where the sound must be said. (lead fix 2026-10-07)
mistakes: Nuqta missing in a voiced shayari: 'ज़ख्म' and 'जख्म' alternate. Fix: one decision for the project.
Hypercorrection: 'ज़ल', 'फ़ूल'. Fix: nuqta only on Perso-Arabic or English-sound words.
Mixed encodings (precomposed and base + U+093C) so find-and-replace misses words. Fix: normalise to NFC.
Six rare Urdu words in one couplet with no gloss. Fix: one rare word and a gloss.
Writing Urdu register as a religion signal in satire or character dialogue. Fix: write the character, not the stereotype.
A Hindi-pronounced sound in a shayari voice-over ('सजा' for 'सज़ा'). Fix: nuqta in the script, checked by ear.
cards.sample:
वक़्त ने जो ज़ख़्म दिए, वो अब तक याद हैं,
पर तेरे ज़िक्र से कुछ ज़ख़्म मुस्कुराने लगे हैं।
ग़म अपना है, ख़ुशी अपनी, फ़ासले भी अपने,
फिर हर शाम क़दम तेरी तरफ़ क्यों जाने लगे हैं?

cards.name: US English
cards.summary: American spelling and conventions: -or, -ize, -er, single l (traveled), license for noun and verb, month-day-year dates, double quotation marks with the period and comma inside, and US vocabulary (faucet, not tap). Use it for US-market clients, SaaS docs written to a US style guide and Google Ads aimed at the US.
use_for: US-market copy: websites, ads, emails, press releases
SaaS and developer documentation written to a US style guide (edit:style_google_dev, edit:style_microsoft)
Google Ads and landing pages aimed at the US
English subtitles for a US delivery (lang:english_subtitles)
avoid: Mixing American, British and Indian spellings in one piece.
Month-day-year dates in copy that readers outside the US will read without a month name: write the month as a word.
Rupee amounts for US readers without a dollar equivalent (lang:india_locale_formats).

sources.title: American and British English spelling differences (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: American patterns: color, organize, center, traveled, license (noun and verb), defense, anemia, program, check, tire, gray, plow, aging

sources.title: Netflix English (USA) Timed Text Style Guide
sources.supports: use U.S. English vocabulary (for example 'running faucet' not 'tap'); times written '9:30 a.m.'

rules: -or: color, labor, honor, favor. (src: spelling differences, Wikipedia)
-ize: organize, realize, recognize. (src: spelling differences, Wikipedia)
-er: center, theater, meter. (src: spelling differences, Wikipedia)
Single l before -ed/-ing: traveled, canceled, labeled, modeling. (src: spelling differences, Wikipedia)
License is both noun and verb; 'defense' takes -se; practice is both noun and verb. (src: spelling differences, Wikipedia)
Other American forms: anemia, program, check (a bank check), tire, gray, plow, aging, catalog. (src: spelling differences, Wikipedia)
Dates are month-day-year ('October 5, 2026'); times are '9:30 a.m.'. (src: Netflix English USA for the time format; date order is general US usage)
US vocabulary, not British: 'faucet', not 'tap'. Also write 'sidewalk', 'truck', 'apartment' for the US reader. (src: Netflix English USA for the faucet example; the other words are general usage)
Double quotation marks; commas and periods go inside the closing quote. (general US usage, unsourced)
Do not mix with UK or Indian spellings in one piece; set the proofing language to English (US) and read the final once. (house practice)
mistakes: 'Organise' and 'color' in one US page. Fix: -ize and -or everywhere.
'Licence' on a US page. Fix: 'license'.
Indian-English phrasing ('prepone', 'revert back') in a US client email. Fix: US plain wording.
'5/10/2026' in a US email to an Indian reader. Fix: 'October 5, 2026'.
Prices in rupees on a page aimed at US buyers. Fix: dollar prices.
Spell-checker left on UK or India settings. Fix: English (US).
cards.sample: Our Austin team will organize a free demo at the center on November 14, 2026. Please bring a valid license for the equipment you plan to test. Parking is free, and our program starts at 9:30 a.m. sharp. Gray badges are for guests; color-coded badges are for staff.
